proposed.text: An architect's building design was published on an international architecture website without the architect's knowledge or consent. The unauthorized publication has been online for three years, and the architect has now discovered it. Does the length of unauthorized publication eliminate the architect's right to pursue enforcement action?

options.text: Yes, because silence for more than two years automatically waives all copyright remedies
Yes, because publication on a public website is always implied authorization
No, delayed discovery does not automatically eliminate enforcement, but damages must be analyzed under RA 8293 proof and timing limits
Only if the website obtained copies from a former client; otherwise no remedy exists

rationale.a: This invents a two-year waiver rule.
rationale.b: Public website posting is not automatically implied authorization.
rationale.d: The identity of the source may matter factually, but RA 8293 remedies are not limited to former-client leaks.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 Section 177 protects communication/display-type economic rights, and Section 216 provides injunction and damages/profits remedies. Section 226 limits damages recovery after four years from the time the cause of action arose. A three-year unauthorized online use does not automatically eliminate enforcement, but the remedy analysis must stay within RA 8293 proof and timing limits.
rationale.takeaway: Delay does not automatically erase enforcement, but damages timing must be checked.

proposed.explanation: Added Section 226 caution to avoid unlimited delayed-discovery language.
